title: Introduction to Velox
description: What Velox is, why it exists, and how it compares to other routers.
content: Velox is a lightweight, high-performance HTTP router for Go. It was designed from the ground up to minimize allocations and maximize throughput for API servers. What makes Velox fast? Velox uses a radix tree for route matching with zero heap allocations on the hot path. Every route lookup completes in sub-microsecond time, regardless of how many routes are registered. Comparison with Other Routers Feature Velox net/http Gorilla Mux Chi Routing Algorithm Radix tree Linear scan Regexp Radix tree Allocations per Request 0 1+ 5+ 0 Path Parameters Yes Go 1.22+ Yes Yes Middleware Built-in chains Manual Manual Built-in Performance Excellent Good Moderate Excellent Architecture Overview graph LR Client[Client] --> Router[Router] Router --> MW1[Middleware 1] MW1 --> MW2[Middleware 2] MW2 --> Handler[Handler] Handler --> Response[Response] The request flows through the router's radix tree, then through the middleware chain, and finally reaches the handler. Each step is zero-allocation on the happy path.

title: Middleware
description: How to write and chain middleware in Velox.
content: Middleware in Velox wraps handlers to add cross-cutting behavior like logging, authentication, and error recovery. Warning Middleware execution order matters. Place authentication middleware before route handlers, and recovery middleware at the outermost layer. Writing a Middleware A middleware is a function that takes a handler and returns a handler: go go func Logger() velox.Middleware { return func(next velox.HandlerFunc) velox.HandlerFunc { return func(c *velox.Context) { start := time.Now() next(c) log.Printf("%s %s %v", c.Method, c.Path, time.Since(start)) } } } func RequireAuth(secret string) velox.Middleware { return func(next velox.HandlerFunc) velox.HandlerFunc { return func(c *velox.Context) { token := c.Header("Authorization") if !validateToken(token, secret) { c.JSON(401, map[string]string{"error": "unauthorized"}) return } next(c) } } } Middleware Signature :::details[Show full middleware type signature]{open} Copy type Middleware func ( HandlerFunc ) HandlerFunc type HandlerFunc func ( * Context ) The Middleware type is a higher-order function: it receives the next handler in the chain and returns a new handler that wraps it. ::: Chaining Middleware Middleware is applied in order. The first middleware added is the outermost wrapper: Copy r := velox . New () r . Use ( Recovery ()) // outermost: catches panics from everything below r . Use ( Logger ()) // logs every request r . Use ( CORS ()) // adds CORS headers r . Use ( Auth ()) // authenticates requests

title: Router
description: The Velox Router type and its methods.
content: The Router is the central type in Velox. It holds the route tree, middleware stack, and configuration. Constructor Function Description New() Creates a new Router with default settings NewWithConfig(cfg Config) Creates a Router with custom configuration Methods HTTP Methods GET , POST , PUT , DELETE , PATCH , HEAD , OPTIONS — register handlers for specific HTTP methods. Middleware Use(mw ...Middleware) — add middleware to the global chain. Applied to all routes in registration order. Groups Group(prefix string) *Group — create a route group with a shared path prefix and middleware stack. Static Files Static(prefix, root string) — serve static files from a directory. Deprecated The Handle(method, path, handler) method is deprecated. Use the typed methods ( GET , POST , etc.) instead.

title: Request
description: Accessing request data in Velox handlers.
content: Velox provides a rich API for reading request data through the Context object. Quick Start Guide See practical request handling examples in the Quick Start guide. → Reading Request Bodies JSON Body Form Data Query Parameters Copy type CreateUser struct { Name string `json:"name"` Email string `json:"email"` } func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { var user CreateUser if err := c . BindJSON ( & user ); err != nil { c . JSON ( 400 , map [ string ] string { "error" : err . Error ()}) return } // use user.Name, user.Email } Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { name := c . FormValue ( "name" ) email := c . FormValue ( "email" ) // use name, email } Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { page := c . QueryInt ( "page" , 1 ) // default: 1 limit := c . QueryInt ( "limit" , 20 ) // default: 20 sort := c . Query ( "sort" ) } Path Parameters Path parameters are defined with a colon prefix in the route pattern: Copy r . GET ( "/users/:id" , func ( c * velox . Context ) { id := c . Param ( "id" ) c . JSON ( 200 , map [ string ] string { "id" : id }) })

title: Request Context
description: Working with request-scoped context values.
content: Every Velox handler receives a *Context object that provides access to the request, response, and request-scoped values. Tip The context is pooled and recycled between requests. Never store a reference to it outside the handler's lifetime. Reading Request Data Access path parameters, query strings, and headers through the context: Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { id := c . Param ( "id" ) // path parameter page := c . Query ( "page" ) // query string auth := c . Header ( "Authorization" ) } Keyboard Shortcuts When using the Velox dev server, these shortcuts are available: Press Ctrl+C to stop the server Press Ctrl+R to reload routes Press Escape to cancel the current operation Important Notes The most critical thing to remember about contexts is that they are not safe for concurrent use . Each handler invocation gets its own context from the pool. Here's something not everyone knows: the context pool uses sync.Pool under the hood, which means contexts may be garbage collected between requests . The router uses a radix tree 1 for efficient path matching. Each node in the tree represents a path segment 2 . Also known as a Patricia trie or compact prefix tree. ↩︎ Path segments are delimited by / characters. ↩︎

title: Response
description: Sending responses from Velox handlers.
content: Velox provides multiple ways to send responses to clients. Response Methods Method Description c.JSON(code, v) Send JSON response with status code c.String(code, s) Send plain text response c.HTML(code, html) Send HTML response c.Blob(code, ct, b) Send binary data with content type c.Redirect(code, url) Send redirect response c.NoContent(code) Send empty response with status code Response Flow Figure 1: Response flow through the middleware chain The response travels back through the middleware chain in reverse order, allowing each middleware to inspect or modify the response before it reaches the client. Streaming Responses For large responses, use the streaming API to avoid buffering the entire response in memory: Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { c . Stream ( 200 , "text/plain" , func ( w io . Writer ) error { for i := 0 ; i < 1000 ; i ++ { fmt . Fprintf ( w , "line %d\n" , i ) } return nil }) }

title: Writing Velox Middleware
description: A practical guide to writing reusable middleware for Velox.
content: Middleware is the backbone of any serious Velox application. This guide covers practical patterns for writing reusable middleware. Performance Characteristics The theoretical throughput of a middleware chain is $O(1)$ per request, since each middleware is a direct function call with no reflection or dynamic dispatch. For a chain with $n$ middleware functions, the total overhead is: $$ $$ In practice, each middleware adds approximately 5-15 nanoseconds of overhead. Middleware { limiter := rate . NewLimiter ( rate . Limit ( rps ), rps ) return func ( next velox . HandlerFunc ) velox . HandlerFunc { return func ( c * velox . Context ) { if ! limiter . Allow () { c . JSON ( 429 , map [ string ] string { "error" : "rate limit exceeded" , }) return } next ( c ) } } }

title: 10 Performance Tips for Velox
description: How to squeeze every last nanosecond out of your Velox application.
content: Here are ten tips to get the most out of your Velox application. Use path parameters instead of query strings for resource identifiers. Path parameters are parsed during route matching at zero additional cost . Minimize middleware per route. Each middleware adds a function call to the chain. Group routes that need the same middleware. Prefer c.JSON() over manual marshaling. The built-in method uses a pooled encoder that avoids allocations. Enable route caching for APIs with repetitive path patterns. Set Config.CacheSize to a power of two. Use c.Stream() for large responses instead of buffering in memory. Profile with pprof to find bottlenecks. Velox integrates with the standard net/http/pprof package. Set appropriate timeouts. Configure ReadTimeout , WriteTimeout , and IdleTimeout on the underlying http.Server . Use connection pooling for database and HTTP client connections. The context pool Velox reuses context objects via sync.Pool to minimize GC pressure is already optimized. Compress responses with the gzip middleware for text-heavy APIs. Benchmark your routes with go test -bench . Velox includes benchmark helpers in the veloxtest package.

title: Middleware Chains
description: Building composable middleware chains with Velox.
content: Middleware chains in Velox are composable function pipelines. Each middleware wraps the next handler in the chain, creating an onion-like structure. Chain Composition Copy func Chain ( middlewares ... Middleware ) Middleware { return func ( next HandlerFunc ) HandlerFunc { for i := len ( middlewares ) - 1 ; i >= 0 ; i -- { next = middlewares [ i ]( next ) } return next } } Route-Specific Middleware Apply middleware to specific routes or groups: Copy r := velox . New () // Global middleware r . Use ( Logger (), Recovery ()) // Group-specific middleware api := r . Group ( "/api" ) api . Use ( Auth ()) api . GET ( "/users" , listUsers ) api . POST ( "/users" , createUser ) // Single-route middleware r . GET ( "/admin" , AdminOnly (), adminHandler )

title: Custom Request Context
description: Extending the request context with custom typed values.
content: Velox contexts can carry request-scoped values that are accessible throughout the middleware chain and handler. Important Context values should only be used for request-scoped data like user identity, request IDs, and tracing spans. Never use them as a substitute for function parameters. Setting Values Copy func AuthMiddleware () velox . Middleware { return func ( next velox . HandlerFunc ) velox . HandlerFunc { return func ( c * velox . Context ) { user := authenticateRequest ( c ) c . Set ( "user" , user ) next ( c ) } } } Reading Values Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { user := c . Get ( "user" ).( * User ) c . JSON ( 200 , user ) } Type-Safe Access For production code, define typed accessor functions: Copy type contextKey string const userKey contextKey = "user" func SetUser ( c * velox . Context , u * User ) { c . Set ( string ( userKey ), u ) } func GetUser ( c * velox . Context ) * User { return c . Get ( string ( userKey )).( * User ) }

title: Handling URL Parameters
description: How to extract and validate URL path parameters.
content: Velox supports three types of URL parameters: path parameters, query parameters, and wildcards. Caution Path parameter names are case-sensitive. :userId and :userid are different parameters. Path Parameters Define parameters with a colon prefix: Copy r . GET ( "/users/:id" , func ( c * velox . Context ) { id := c . Param ( "id" ) c . JSON ( 200 , map [ string ] string { "user_id" : id }) }) Query Parameters Access query string values through the context: Copy r . GET ( "/search" , func ( c * velox . Context ) { q := c . Query ( "q" ) page := c . QueryInt ( "page" , 1 ) c . JSON ( 200 , map [ string ] any { "query" : q , "page" : page }) }) Parameter Validation Velox does not validate parameter types automatically. You should validate and convert parameters in your handler: Copy id , err := strconv . Atoi ( c . Param ( "id" )) if err != nil { c . JSON ( 400 , map [ string ] string { "error" : "invalid id" }) return }

title: Middleware
description: How to write and chain middleware in Velox.
content: Middleware in Velox wraps handlers to add cross-cutting behavior like logging, authentication, and error recovery. Warning Middleware execution order matters. Place authentication middleware before route handlers, and recovery middleware at the outermost layer. Writing a Middleware A middleware is a function that takes a handler and returns a handler: go go func Logger() velox.Middleware { return func(next velox.HandlerFunc) velox.HandlerFunc { return func(c *velox.Context) { start := time.Now() next(c) log.Printf("%s %s %v", c.Method, c.Path, time.Since(start)) } } } func RequireAuth(secret string) velox.Middleware { return func(next velox.HandlerFunc) velox.HandlerFunc { return func(c *velox.Context) { token := c.Header("Authorization") if !validateToken(token, secret) { c.JSON(401, map[string]string{"error": "unauthorized"}) return } next(c) } } } Middleware Signature :::details[Show full middleware type signature]{open} Copy type Middleware func ( HandlerFunc ) HandlerFunc type HandlerFunc func ( * Context ) The Middleware type is a higher-order function: it receives the next handler in the chain and returns a new handler that wraps it. ::: Chaining Middleware Middleware is applied in order. The first middleware added is the outermost wrapper: Copy r := velox . New () r . Use ( Recovery ()) // outermost: catches panics from everything below r . Use ( Logger ()) // logs every request r . Use ( CORS ()) // adds CORS headers r . Use ( Auth ()) // authenticates requests

title: Request Context
description: Working with request-scoped context values.
content: Every Velox handler receives a *Context object that provides access to the request, response, and request-scoped values. Tip The context is pooled and recycled between requests. Never store a reference to it outside the handler's lifetime. Reading Request Data Access path parameters, query strings, and headers through the context: Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { id := c . Param ( "id" ) // path parameter page := c . Query ( "page" ) // query string auth := c . Header ( "Authorization" ) } Keyboard Shortcuts When using the Velox dev server, these shortcuts are available: Press Ctrl+C to stop the server Press Ctrl+R to reload routes Press Escape to cancel the current operation Important Notes The most critical thing to remember about contexts is that they are not safe for concurrent use . Each handler invocation gets its own context from the pool. Here's something not everyone knows: the context pool uses sync.Pool under the hood, which means contexts may be garbage collected between requests . The router uses a radix tree 1 for efficient path matching. Each node in the tree represents a path segment 2 . Also known as a Patricia trie or compact prefix tree. ↩︎ Path segments are delimited by / characters. ↩︎

JSON ( 400 , map [ string ] string { "error" : "invalid id" }) return }

title: 10 Performance Tips for Velox
description: How to squeeze every last nanosecond out of your Velox application.
content: Here are ten tips to get the most out of your Velox application. Use path parameters instead of query strings for resource identifiers. Path parameters are parsed during route matching at zero additional cost . Minimize middleware per route. Each middleware adds a function call to the chain. Group routes that need the same middleware. Prefer c.JSON() over manual marshaling. The built-in method uses a pooled encoder that avoids allocations. Enable route caching for APIs with repetitive path patterns. Set Config.CacheSize to a power of two. Use c.Stream() for large responses instead of buffering in memory. Profile with pprof to find bottlenecks. Velox integrates with the standard net/http/pprof package. Set appropriate timeouts. Configure ReadTimeout , WriteTimeout , and IdleTimeout on the underlying http.Server . Use connection pooling for database and HTTP client connections. The context pool Velox reuses context objects via sync.Pool to minimize GC pressure is already optimized. Compress responses with the gzip middleware for text-heavy APIs. Benchmark your routes with go test -bench . Velox includes benchmark helpers in the veloxtest package.

content: Velox provides multiple ways to send responses to clients. title: 10 Performance Tips for Velox
description: How to squeeze every last nanosecond out of your Velox application.
content: Here are ten tips to get the most out of your Velox application. Use path parameters instead of query strings for resource identifiers. Path parameters are parsed during route matching at zero additional cost . Minimize middleware per route. Each middleware adds a function call to the chain. Group routes that need the same middleware. Prefer c.JSON() over manual marshaling. The built-in method uses a pooled encoder that avoids allocations. Enable route caching for APIs with repetitive path patterns. Set Config.CacheSize to a power of two. Use c.Stream() for large responses instead of buffering in memory. Profile with pprof to find bottlenecks. Velox integrates with the standard net/http/pprof package. Set appropriate timeouts. Configure ReadTimeout , WriteTimeout , and IdleTimeout on the underlying http.Server . Use connection pooling for database and HTTP client connections. The context pool Velox reuses context objects via sync.Pool to minimize GC pressure is already optimized. Compress responses with the gzip middleware for text-heavy APIs. Benchmark your routes with go test -bench . Velox includes benchmark helpers in the veloxtest package.

title: Request Context
description: Working with request-scoped context values.
content: Every Velox handler receives a *Context object that provides access to the request, response, and request-scoped values. Tip The context is pooled and recycled between requests. Never store a reference to it outside the handler's lifetime. Reading Request Data Access path parameters, query strings, and headers through the context: Copy func handler ( c * velox . Context ) { id := c . Param ( "id" ) // path parameter page := c . Query ( "page" ) // query string auth := c . Header ( "Authorization" ) } Keyboard Shortcuts When using the Velox dev server, these shortcuts are available: Press Ctrl+C to stop the server Press Ctrl+R to reload routes Press Escape to cancel the current operation Important Notes The most critical thing to remember about contexts is that they are not safe for concurrent use . Each handler invocation gets its own context from the pool. Here's something not everyone knows: the context pool uses sync.Pool under the hood, which means contexts may be garbage collected between requests . The router uses a radix tree 1 for efficient path matching. Each node in the tree represents a path segment 2 . Also known as a Patricia trie or compact prefix tree. ↩︎ Path segments are delimited by / characters. ↩︎
